newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria rulers agree polls, economic crisis stays.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria rulers agree polls, economic crisis stays.

text.p: Bulgaria's ex-communist rulers bowed to 30 days of mass protests, agreeing to elections by April 20, but President Petar Stoyanov warned a political settlement would not ease an economic crisis.
Thousands of opposition supporters turned roadblocks into street parties, celebrating late into the night despite sub-zero temperatures.
Protesters dismantled barricades and cars flying opposition flags drove through the streets honking their horns.

A joint statement issued after a meeting of political leaders on Tuesday said all parties in parliament had agreed not to try to form a government and the president would schedule elections in the second 10 days of April.
Under the constitution, Stoyanov must appoint a caretaker cabinet whose main role will be to organise the polls.
"We cannot expect that the deep economic crisis in Bulgaria can be resolved in two, three, or five months," Stoyanov said.
"I cannot and have never promised that living conditions in Bulgaria will improve in the short term. We are faced with many, many difficulties created by the governance so far."
Hundreds of students and teenagers danced to a rock group in front of the gold-domed Alexander Nevski Cathedral, the site of daily opposition rallies for the past month.
UDF leader Ivan Kostov invited supporters to one last celebratory victory rally on Wednesday evening.
"I am happy that bloodshed was avoided, I feared a violent crackdown," said accountant Anna Petrova.

"There is still a great deal of uncertainty. The fuel shortages, bread queues, astronomical prices and meagre wages will be still here for some time, but there is hope," said software expert Petar Bonev.
Inflation was estimated at 50 percent in January, Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery is running out of crude because it cannot pay its bills, and people queued for bread in the capital on Tuesday.
"I do not promise you that you will be richer or you will live better, I promise you that under the next government I will be honest and you will be master of your lives," Stoyanov told the crowd.

The Socialists, elected to a four-year term in December 1994, have been blamed for the severe economic crisis. Outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21 but the party had insisted on forming a new cabinet.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) stepped up strikes a week ago, when the Socialists said they would form a new cabinet.

Protesters in the town of Doupnitsa have kept up a round-the-clock blockade of main road and rail routes to Greece since last Wednesday. They said on Tuesday night they would rename one barricade site Victory Square.
Late-night transport resumed in Sofia after a two-day strike.
Putting a brave face on the climbdown, Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) leader Georgi Parvanov said the agreement showed the party's political maturity.
"This was a step towards restoration of confidence in the BSP and its effect will be felt in the upcoming elections," he told reporters.
The political crisis has accelerated the collapse of the national currency, which closed at 2,800-3,000 levs to the dollar on Tuesday from 1,000 a week ago.
The International Monetary Fund welcomed Bulgaria's decision and voiced hopes for the resumption of loan talks. An IMF official said a mission would arrive as soon as a new government was in place.
